title: Patchbench field sketch + customer garden notes
content:
Purpose: quick, rough synthesis of 8 recent customer threads (Nov 2025–Feb 2026) focused on token-cost surprises and correctness regressions when customers use long-conversation chat + embeddings pipelines. Use this as a lightweight scout for engineering/prod-probe ideas and quick patch experiments.

Quick TL;DR
- Recurring asks: better visibility into per-route token amplification (embeddings + summarize + chat), safer defaults for KV cache TTLs, and a lightweight knob to prefer low-cost model variants when tail latency spikes.
- Common pain: customers report 20–60% sudden token volume increases after adding a short summarization step; hard to trace because telemetry ties to route but not composite prompt graphs.
- Near-term probes proposed: (A) route-level token waterfall (cheap UI) + sample trace export; (B) opt-in prefix-cache visualization and TTL override; (C) skyline experiment: controlled fallback to 8-bit quantized variant on capacity pressure.

Signal snippets (verbatim-ish)
- "We turned on auto-summarize and overnight our bill jumped; logs show same number of API calls but tokens doubled — where are they?" — fintech startup (enterprise dedicated)
- "When we pin a model it's fine; but occasional fallback to smaller model returns worse hallucination rates. We need safe fallbacks or regression guardrails." — analytics platform (hosted)
- "Embedding + chat pipeline is opaque; we have to stitch logs across three services to understand why token count exploded on a single user flow." — doc management SaaS (private)

Pattern map (rough)
1) Composite prompts not attributed: customers call the API in a pipeline (embed -> retrieve -> summarize -> chat). Our billing and traces show only the final route. Result: Hard to tie a spike to the summarize step.
2) KV cache TTL friction: default short TTLs + small cache budgets for multi-tenant setups mean many re-computes of context when a user returns within a short window. Many customers prefer longer TTLs for session-heavy apps.
3) Fallback regressions: automatic model fallback to lower-capacity variants saves cost but sometimes fails quality checks and triggers rollback. Customers want predictable quality fallbacks and a way to label fallbacks as "safe" vs "best-effort."

Proposed low-effort experiments (ranked)
- Experiment 1: Token Waterfall Export (0.5–1 sprint)
  - What: route-level breakdown showing tokens per pipeline stage (we stitch client-side with minimal SDK change — add optional header with pipeline-stage-id; server will echo and tally). Export sample traces as CSV for customers.
  - Why: immediate troubleshooting aid, reduces support ticket back-and-forth.
  - Risks: small SDK churn; sampling privacy checks needed for PII.
  - Success metric: reduction in cs-ticket cycle-time for token-related billing escalations by 40% in pilot customers.

- Experiment 2: TTL Advisory + Override (1 sprint + small UI)
  - What: surface current KV cache TTLs in Console per-customer/route and allow CS to propose (and user to accept) temporary overrides for session-heavy customers.
  - Why: fixes most repeated recompute situations without infra changes.
  - Tech note: need guardrail to force eviction after X days; expose per-tenant limits.
  - Success metric: decreased repeat computation RPS for pilots; anecdotal customer feedback.

- Experiment 3: Quantized-fallback Canary (2 sprints + infra)
  - What: support an opt-in policy to route to an 8-bit quantized variant when tail latency or capacity thresholds are hit. Add qualitative Q/A sampling and mismatch monitoring to detect hallucination/regression.
  - Why: closer to production-grade inexpensive fallback; can reduce committed GPU pressure and cost.
  - Downside: regression risk; requires eval harness and quick rollback.
  - Success metric: unit-token-cost drop during bursts without >2x QA-detected regressions.

Engineering notes / quick feasibility comments (from Jonah + Marco)
- Token-waterfall: feasible with minimal server change; need SDK header to annotate stage name. For third-party SDKs, provide a thin shim in Console that can reformat requests.
- TTL override: Console knob to set tenancy-level TTLs is straightforward; must integrate with existing cache eviction pipeline (SRE to weigh in).
- Quantized fallback: infra work to maintain model variant pool + routing policy; reuse existing smart-routing stub but add deterministic canary. We should avoid automatic fallback for routes with "quality_strict=true" tag.

Customer impact scoring (subjective)
- Fintech enterprise (token attribution & TTL controls): high impact — immediate pain due to costs + auditability.
- SMB doc-saas (embedding pollution): medium — prefers workable telemetry and TTL tuning.
- Analytics-platform (fallback regressions): high — quality regressions harm core product outputs.

Open questions / unknowns
- Privacy: token waterfall traces may include user content unless sanitized. Can we export only counts + hashes? CS needs explicit guidance for PII-sensitive customers.
- Pricing/contract implications: if we expose TTL overrides that reduce unit-cost, how does this affect usage tiers and billing? Finance should weigh in for entitlements.
- Evaluation: what constitutes an acceptable regression for fallback models? Should be per-customer SLA-defined.

Suggested immediate next steps (this week)
- Share this note with product-hosted-api, eng-serving-runtime, and SRE. (Priya to run a 30-min sync Wed 2/18).
- Kickoff a 2-week pilot for Token Waterfall with 3 customers: fintech enterprise, doc-saas, analytics-platform. Jonah to draft SDK header RFC by Mon 2/15.
- CS prepare a short customer comms template explaining the Token Waterfall pilot and data privacy safeguards.

Notes-to-self / scratch items (choppy)
- Sketch of CSV columns for waterfall: request_id, stage_name, tokens_sent, tokens_received, model_variant, timestamp, sample_hash
- Slack thread where fintech raised issue: #cs-billing-escapes /msg 1339
- Possible quick patch: console shows estimated tokens for a route when editing steps (cheap UX lift)

Appendix: sample customer trace (anonymized) — single user flow
- call 1 embed (2.1k tokens) -> index -> call 2 retrieve (0.2k tokens) -> call 3 summarize (7.8k tokens) -> call 4 chat (1.2k tokens). Billing shows final route only (chat 1.2k) so embedded costs invisible.

If you want to run protos or need me to draft the SDK header RFC I can take first pass. This doc deliberately unstructured — meant to be a fast field notebook for CS + eng to run lightweight probes.

Asha P.
CS (patchbench scout)
